Lesson overview:
- Level: A0 General English
- Unit: Unit 8. People around you
- Time: 60 min (Essential) / 90 min (Expanded) / 120 min (Full Workshop)
- Focus: Remarkable people
- Materials: Photos of famous people, ability cards, award certificate, COSYmanuals 'can/can't' and 'present simple' pages.
By the end of this lesson, you can:

• express talent and abilities with modal can/can't
• describe famous achievements

Which word belongs to the previous lesson?
Core Active Vocabulary (10 items):

famous — known by many people. Example: She is a famous singer.
talent — a natural ability. Example: He has a talent for music.
can — a modal verb for ability. Example: I can swim.
speak — to say words. Example: She can speak three languages.
write — to make words on paper or a screen. Example: He can write stories.
sing — to make music with your voice. Example: She can sing very well.
play — to do a sport or game. Example: He can play football.
achieve — to succeed in doing something. Example: She achieved her goal.
record — the best result ever. Example: He holds a world record.
work — a job or activity you do. Example: I work in an office.
Essential Chunks & Functional Collocations:

• He can speak four languages. (describing ability)
• She can sing very well. (describing ability)
• He is a famous writer. (describing a person)
• They can play football. (describing ability)
• What can he do? (asking about ability)
• He achieved a world record. (describing an achievement)
Vocabulary practice: choose the correct word.
Which word means 'known by many people'?
Which word means 'a natural ability'?
Complete the sentence with a word from the list.
Pronunciation Focus: The /k/ sound in 'can' and weak forms in questions

can /kən/ — weak form in sentences
famous /ˈfeɪməs/ — stress the first syllable
talent /ˈtælənt/ — stress the first syllable
achieve /əˈtʃiːv/ — stress the second syllable

He can speak four languages. She can sing very well.

elements.content: Grammar Focus: Use 'can' to talk about ability, possibility, and requests; use 'can't' for inability.

Form:
Can / can't: Subject + can + base verb. Negative: cannot / can't. Question: Can you...? Yes, I can. / No, I can't.

Examples:
• I can speak English.
• She can swim very well.
• He can't drive.
• Can you help me?
Controlled practice: choose the correct form.
She ___ speak three languages.
I ___ drive a car.
___ you swim?
He can ___ very fast.
Substitution drill: say the sentence with the new words.

• I can ... (speak / swim / cook).
• I can't ... (drive / dance / sing).
• Can you ...?
Question-answer practice: ask and answer with your partner.

• What can you do well?
• What can't you do?
• Can your best friend cook?
Personalised production: use the structure about your own life.

• Write three sentences with 'can' about your abilities.
• Write three sentences with 'can't' about things you cannot do.
Reading: Remarkable people

He is a famous writer. He can speak four languages and write remarkable stories. She is a singer. She can sing very well and play the piano. They are athletes. They can run fast and jump high. They achieved a world record. Remarkable people work hard and never give up. What can you do?
What can the writer do?
options: speak four languages and write stories

elements.content: What did the athletes achieve?
Listening: listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.

A: What can she do?
B: She can sing very well and play the piano.
A: Can she speak other languages?
B: Yes, she can. She speaks three languages.
A: Is she famous?
B: Yes, she is. She is a remarkable singer.
What can the singer do?
How many languages does she speak?
Speaking task: Present a remarkable person to your partner. Say what they can do and why you admire them.

• Who is a remarkable person in your life?
• What can they do?
• Can you sing or play an instrument?
• What talent do you want to have?
• Why do people admire famous people?
Role-play: You are presenting an award to a remarkable person. Introduce them and describe their abilities.
Work in pairs. Take turns. Use at least five target words and one target grammar structure. Then swap roles.
Writing task: Write five sentences about a remarkable person using 'can/can't'.
Model: He/She can ... He/She can't ... He/She is ...
